blocks.text: 6.What are the parameters measured by spirometry? (mobilizable volumes)
?Vital capacity (CV): volume of air mobilized by
a forced expiration following a forced inspiration.
?The maximum expiratory volume/second (FEV): it is the fraction of the vital capacity (CV) expired in 1 second by rapid and forced expiration.
? The FEV/CV ratio determines the Tiffeneau index (TI)
?Peripheral flow rates
normalized: flow rates normalized to a percentage of CV measured at a point on the forced expiration curve.
7.Define non-mobilizable volumes
7.Define non-mobilizable volumes
?Residual volume (VR): volume of air that remains in the lung after
forced expiration =1.2 - 1.5L
?Functional residual capacity (CRF): this is the volume of air that remains
into the lung after normal expiration. CRF=ERV+VR
?Total lung capacity (CPT): this is the volume of air contained in the
lungs after forced inspiration. CPT=CV+VR =ERV+VRI+Vt+VR= 5,500 ml.

blocks.text: How to perform spirometry?
? The nose is closed with a nose clip,
? the patient breathes calmly,
? then we ask him to breathe deeply: he inhales, deeply, and then exhales as hard and as quickly as possible all the air from his lungs into the spirometer.
How to perform spirometry?
?Exhalation duration should be at least 6 seconds.
? Care should be taken to avoid perioral leaks.
?These simple maneuvers make it possible to measure lung volumes.
?To measure forced expiratory flow rates, the patient is asked to take in as much air as possible and then blow as hard and as long as they can to empty all the air they have in their lungs.
Curves obtained

? the volume-time curve ? the flow-volume curve, the appearance of which makes it possible to judge whether or not the maneuver was carried out correctly and to suggest a ventilatory disorder. ? The results depend not only on the technique itself but also on its execution by the patient, who in the absence of good coordination and/or motivation risks being underestimated.
